clinicalPearls: Caused by dominant variants in TNPO3 encoding transportin-3, a nuclear import receptor; the D-prefix denotes autosomal dominant inheritance, unlike the recessive R-subtypes.
The disease-causing change characteristically affects the stop codon or adjacent sequence, producing an abnormally extended transportin-3 protein with a toxic gain-of-function effect.
Inheritance is dominant, so a positive family history across generations is typical and helps separate it from the recessive limb-girdle subtypes.
Age at onset is strikingly wide even within one family, spanning early childhood to late adulthood.
Weakness is proximal and limb-girdle in distribution, and distal involvement as well as respiratory muscle weakness can develop as the disease advances.
Serum creatine kinase is usually normal or only modestly raised, in contrast with the very high values seen in sarcoglycanopathy or dysferlinopathy.
The originally described large kindred was of Italian and Spanish origin, and reports remain relatively rare worldwide.
reference.pathophysiology: LGMD D2 is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in TNPO3 on chromosome 7q32, encoding transportin-3, a member of the importin-beta family that mediates nuclear import of serine/arginine-rich splicing factors and other cargo. The characteristic disease alleles disrupt the natural termination of the protein, generating a C-terminally extended transportin-3 that acts through a dominant, gain-of-function or dominant-negative mechanism rather than simple haploinsufficiency. The abnormal protein is thought to perturb nucleocytoplasmic trafficking and the handling of splicing factors within myonuclei, with mislocalisation of transportin-3 and disturbed RNA-processing pathways in muscle. This produces a chronic myopathy with proximal-predominant weakness; the dominant mechanism and the highly variable age at onset distinguish it mechanistically from the recessive structural sarcolemmal defects of the R-subtypes.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal dominant limb-girdle subtypes such as LGMD D1 (DNAJB6) and LGMD D3 (HNRNPDL)
Recessive limb-girdle subtypes (LGMD R1 calpainopathy, R2 dysferlinopathy) when family history is unclear
Myotonic dystrophy given multisystem dominant inheritance
Late-onset Pompe disease with proximal and respiratory weakness
Inclusion body and other rimmed-vacuole myopathies
Congenital or dominant myopathies with wide intrafamilial variability
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase (often normal or only mildly elevated)
Detailed multigenerational family history and examination of relatives
Muscle MRI to characterise the pattern of selective muscle involvement
Muscle biopsy, which may show myopathic changes and rimmed vacuoles
Targeted TNPO3 sequencing focusing on the terminal region, or a comprehensive LGMD gene panel
Pulmonary function testing where respiratory involvement is suspected
redFlags: Emerging respiratory muscle weakness with symptoms of nocturnal hypoventilation
Progression to loss of independent ambulation
New swallowing difficulty suggesting bulbar or more widespread involvement
Unexplained functional decline warranting reassessment of the pattern of weakness
reference.prognosis: Progression is generally slow but the course is highly variable, mirroring the wide range in age at onset, so some individuals remain mildly affected while others develop substantial proximal weakness. Long-term outlook is influenced chiefly by the degree of respiratory muscle involvement.
pitfalls: Excluding a muscular dystrophy because creatine kinase is normal or only mildly raised
Overlooking the dominant inheritance and failing to take a detailed family history
Expecting a uniform age at onset when intrafamilial variability is a hallmark
Missing the specific stop-codon-region variant if TNPO3 analysis does not cover the terminal sequence
references: Peer-reviewed limb-girdle muscular dystrophy classification and consensus statements
management: Recognise there is no disease-modifying pharmacotherapy and use physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain proximal strength, prevent contractures and supply orthoses and aids
Provide pulmonary function surveillance with non-invasive ventilation for the respiratory-muscle weakness that can develop as disease advances
Undertake periodic cardiac assessment with ECG and echocardiography
Deliver multidisciplinary neuromuscular rehabilitation adapted to the highly variable rate of progression
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, assessing affected relatives across generations
